slides.text: There is a huge number of different models based on the CNN idea.
Most of these models are accompanied by code.
Many of these models provide models pretrained on ImageNet or other large standard datasets.
These models are usually based on a few standard ideas, which will now be considered.
AlexNet (Krizhevsky, Sutskever, Hinton, 2012) is the architecture that kick-started modern deep learning for computer vision.
VGG (Oxford Visual Geometry Group) represents large convolutions as compositions of $3 \times 3$ convolutions.
Replacing large convolutions with compositions of $3 \times 3$ convolutions in VGG reduces the number of weights.
Replacing large convolutions with compositions of $3 \times 3$ convolutions makes the network deeper.
The VGG network was used in the ImageNet Large Scale Visual Recognition Competition (ILSVRC-2014).
NVIDIA has been optimising GPUs especially for $3 \times 3$ convolutions.
Inception and GoogLeNet use the 'network in network' idea.
Inception and GoogLeNet use the 'network in network' idea to reduce the number of weights even further compared to earlier architectures.
Another idea in Inception/GoogLeNet is to add additional classifiers, which add additional terms to the objective function.
In Inception v2 (Szegedy et al., 2015), $n \times n$ convolutions were replaced by $n \times 1$ and $1 \times n$ convolutions.
Filter banks in Inception v2 became wide rather than deep.
The same paper (Szegedy et al., 2015) introduced Inception v3.
Inception v3 uses RMSProp.
Inception v3 uses factorised $7 \times 7$ convolutions.
Inception v3 uses batch normalisation in the additional classifiers.
Inception v3 uses label smoothing.
In a regular classifier, the softmax is trained with a hard objective $q(k) = [k = y]$, which is an indicator that $k$ equals the true label $y$.
The hard objective $q(k) = [k = y]$ causes the arguments of the softmax function to grow unboundedly.
As a result of the hard objective, models overfit and become too certain.
A possible solution is label smoothing, which optimises $q'(k) = (1 - \epsilon)[k = y] + \epsilon\, u(k)$ for some prior distribution $u(k)$.
An example of a prior distribution for label smoothing is $u(k) = \frac{1}{K}$.
Residual learning trains the differences (residues) between one layer and the next, instead of learning a function directly.
A residual unit function is $y^{(k)} = F(x^{(k)}) + x^{(k)}$, where $x^{(k)}$ is the input, $F$ is the layer's function, and $y^{(k)}$ is the output that becomes $x^{(k+1)}$ for the next layer.

The gradient of the residual unit with respect to the input is $\frac{\partial y^{(k)}}{\partial x^{(k)}} = 1 + \frac{\partial F(x^{(k)})}{\partial x^{(k)}}$, so the gradient does not vanish when $F$ saturates.
Residual learning has allowed for very deep networks.
Highway networks (Jürgen Schmidhuber) also represent the output as a combination of $x^{(k)}$ and $F(x^{(k)})$.
In highway networks, the output is $y^{(k)} = C(x^{(k)}) x^{(k)} + T(x^{(k)}) F(x^{(k)})$, with $C$ the carry gate and $T$ the transform gate; typically $C = 1 - T$.
Practice shows that residual connections should be as 'straight' as possible.
ResNet variations and the revolution of depth (Kaiming He) further demonstrated the power of extremely deep convolutional networks.
ResNeXt (Xie et al., 2016) replaces ResNet units with 'split-transform-merge' units, similar to Inception.
In ResNeXt, the input is divided into blocks with respect to channels, and each block receives its own convolutions.
The 'split-transform-merge' idea in ResNeXt is reminiscent of group convolutions.
Group convolutions were used in AlexNet for parallelisation.
Group convolutions yield a kind of specialisation in the resulting feature maps.
Inception v4 and Inception‑ResNet were introduced in a classic paper (Szegedy et al., 2016).
Inception v4 standardises everything and simplifies the units.
Inception v4 defines a 'stem' module first.
Inception v4 uses three basic blocks – A, B, and C – together with special reduction blocks to reduce spatial dimensions.
Inception‑ResNet adds residual connections to Inception blocks.
Inception‑ResNet has no pooling but uses reduction blocks.
Inception‑ResNet has a simpler architecture than previous Inception versions.
Inception‑ResNet v2 is a refined version that performs very well in practice.
SqueezeNet (Iandola et al., 2017) aims to drastically reduce the number of parameters.
SqueezeNet replaces $3 \times 3$ filters with $1 \times 1$ filters.
SqueezeNet reduces the number of input channels for the remaining $3 \times 3$ convolutions.
SqueezeNet delays downsampling as late as possible to keep activation maps large.
The key building block of SqueezeNet is the fire module.
The fire module consists of a squeeze convolutional layer with only $1 \times 1$ filters and an expand layer with a mix of $1 \times 1$ and $3 \times 3$ filters.
SqueezeNet yields about 50× fewer parameters than AlexNet.
There is a trade-off in accuracy with SqueezeNet's parameter reduction.
MobileNet (Howard et al., 2017) designs networks for mobile devices.
MobileNet uses depthwise separable convolutions.
Depthwise separable convolutions decompose a standard convolution into a depthwise convolution (one filter per input channel) followed by a $1 \times 1$ convolution.
The resulting depthwise separable convolution layer has a more complex structure but far fewer weights than a standard convolution.
The overall MobileNet architecture is not very deep.
MobileNet saves many parameters at the price of a small decrease in quality.
EfficientNet (Tan, Le, 2019) applies neural architecture search to design state‑of‑the‑art networks at a fraction of the cost.
A key insight of EfficientNet is compound scaling.
Compound scaling simultaneously scales network width, depth, and input resolution.
Simultaneously scaling width, depth, and resolution yields better performance than scaling a single dimension.
In deep networks, changing the weights of a layer changes the distribution of its outputs.
When the output distribution of a layer changes, the next layer must re-train almost from scratch because it did not expect the new outputs.
Neurons may have already reached saturation, which slows down re-training.
This phenomenon is called internal covariate shift.
Internal covariate shift seriously impedes learning.
Whitening after every layer is a naïve solution to internal covariate shift.
In the example of a layer that adds a bias $b$ to input $u$, normalizing by subtracting the mean yields $\hat{x} = x - \mathbb{E}[x]$.
If the bias is updated by $\Delta b$, the normalized output remains unchanged: $u + b + \Delta b - \mathbb{E}[u + b + \Delta b] = u + b - \mathbb{E}[u + b]$.
As a result, biases will grow unboundedly without affecting the normalized output, causing training to fail.
Normalisation as a layer, $\hat{x} = \text{Norm}(x, X)$, requires the entire dataset $X$ to compute gradients and the covariance matrix.
Full-dataset normalisation is computationally prohibitive.
Batch normalisation normalises each component separately over the current mini-batch.
For a component $x_k$, batch normalisation computes $\hat{x}_k = \frac{x_k - \mathbb{E}[x_k]}{\sqrt{\text{Var}[x_k]}}$, where the statistics are over the mini-batch.
A problem with batch normalisation is that normalised values often fall into the linear region of activation functions, causing nonlinearities to disappear.
To address the linearization problem, learnable shift and scale parameters $\gamma_k$ and $\beta_k$ are introduced: $y_k = \gamma_k \hat{x}_k + \beta_k$.
The parameters $\gamma_k$ and $\beta_k$ are trained jointly with the network weights.
Subsequent research showed that batch normalization's effectiveness does not really depend on reducing internal covariate shift.
Batch normalization helps with regularisation.
Batch normalization makes dropout unnecessary.
Batch normalization improves training.
One possible explanation is that batch normalization smooths the gradients, reducing the Lipschitz constant (Santurkar et al., 2019).
Another possible explanation is that batch normalization decouples the learning of the direction and length of weight vectors, improving training.
There are results showing that batch normalization helps achieve linear convergence in ordinary gradient descent.
Many normalisation methods share the same general operations: compute statistics over a set, normalise, then transform with learned scale and shift parameters.
Normalisation methods differ in which dimensions the statistics are computed over.
Batch normalization computes statistics over the mini-batch dimension $N$.
Batch normalization is commonly used for images.
Layer normalization computes statistics over all channels and spatial dimensions of a layer (all features of a sample).
Layer normalization is used mostly for vectors, in particular in transformers.
Instance normalization computes statistics over the spatial dimensions $H$ and $W$, separately for each sample and channel.
Instance normalization is used, for example, in AdaIN for style transfer.
Group normalization splits channels into groups and normalises over each group together with the spatial dimensions.
Weight standardization standardizes the weights per output channel instead of normalising activations.
Weight standardization effectively normalises the gradients during backpropagation.
Group normalization and weight standardization were used together in BiT (Big Transfer).
Batch normalisation is not effective for recurrent networks (Laurent et al., 2016).
Recurrent batch normalisation was proposed (Cooijmans et al., 2016) to address the ineffectiveness of batch normalization in recurrent networks.

Weight normalisation (Salimans and Kingma, 2016) transforms weights as $h_i = f\left(\frac{\gamma}{\|w_i\|} w_i^\top x + b_i\right)$, which rescales the gradient, stabilises its norm, and brings the covariance matrix closer to the identity.
The landscape of normalisation methods is extensive and remains an active area of research (Huang et al., 2020).
Sequences, such as financial time series, language, and sound, give rise to various problems including sequence classification, sequence labelling, and sequence generation.
A simple approach to sequence processing is to use a sliding window over the sequence.
A more powerful idea is to maintain a hidden state that is updated as the network processes the sequence, leading to recurrent neural networks (RNNs).
In RNNs, the computational graph appears to have cycles.
Backpropagation in RNNs is possible by 'unrolling' the recurrence in time.
Unrolling yields a very deep network with many shared weights.
This deep unrolled network causes notorious training difficulties.
A simple RNN step is defined by: $a_t = b + W s_{t-1} + U x_t$, $s_t = f(a_t)$, $o_t = c + V s_t$, $y_t = h(o_t)$, where $f$ is the recurrent nonlinearity and $h$ the output function.
RNNs suffer from exploding gradients.
RNNs suffer from vanishing gradients.
Exploding gradients in RNNs occur because repeatedly multiplying by the same weight matrix $W$ causes exponential growth in the gradient norm.
Gradient clipping bounds the gradients from above to prevent extreme updates.
One gradient clipping method is clip by norm, e.g., `clipnorm=1.`
Another gradient clipping method is clip by value, e.g., `clipvalue=0.05`.
Pascanu et al. (2013) illustrated gradient clipping and showed that RNNs have 'bifurcation points' where instabilities originate.
A bidirectional RNN uses context from both past and future.
A bidirectional RNN computes forward hidden state $s_t = \sigma(b + W s_{t-1} + U x_t)$ and backward hidden state $s'_t = \sigma(b' + W' s'_{t+1} + U' x_t)$.
The bidirectional RNN output combines both directions: $o_t = c + V s_t + V' s'_t$, $y_t = h(o_t)$.
The principle of bidirectional recurrence generalises to any recurrent architecture.
Vanishing gradients in RNNs occur because the gradient repeatedly passes through multiplication by $W$.
To provide long-term memory, a 'constant error carousel' (a shortcut for gradients) is needed, similar to residual connections in ResNet.
LSTM was developed in the mid-1990s (Hochreiter & Schmidhuber, 1995, 1997; modern form by Gers & Schmidhuber, 2000).
LSTM constructs a more complex unit that explicitly controls memory.
The LSTM cell maintains a cell state $c_t$ and a hidden state $h_t$.
The candidate cell state in LSTM is $c'_t = \tanh(W_{xc} x_t + W_{hc} h_{t-1} + b_{c'})$.
The input gate $i_t$ is $i_t = \sigma(W_{xi} x_t + W_{hi} h_{t-1} + b_i)$.
The forget gate $f_t$ is $f_t = \sigma(W_{xf} x_t + W_{hf} h_{t-1} + b_f)$.
The output gate $o_t$ is $o_t = \sigma(W_{xo} x_t + W_{ho} h_{t-1} + b_o)$.
The cell state update is $c_t = f_t \odot c_{t-1} + i_t \odot c'_t$.
The hidden state is $h_t = o_t \odot \tanh(c_t)$.

When the forget gate is fully open ($f_t = 1$), the cell state update becomes $c_t = c_{t-1} + i_t \odot c'_t$, leading to $\frac{\partial c_t}{\partial c_{t-1}} = 1$, which is the constant error carousel.
In standard LSTM, the gates only see $h_{t-1} = o_{t-1} \odot \tanh(c_{t-1})$.
If the output gate $o_{t-1}$ is closed, the LSTM behaviour becomes independent of the cell state $c_{t-1}$.
Peephole connections add the cell state directly to the gate computations.
Input gate with peephole: $i_t = \sigma(W_{xi} x_t + W_{hi} h_{t-1} + W_{pi} c_{t-1} + b_i)$.
Forget gate with peephole: $f_t = \sigma(W_{xf} x_t + W_{hf} h_{t-1} + W_{pf} c_{t-1} + b_f)$.
Output gate with peephole: $o_t = \sigma(W_{xo} x_t + W_{ho} h_{t-1} + W_{po} c_{t-1} + b_o)$.
There are numerous LSTM variations.
One can remove or add gates, peepholes, activation functions, etc. in LSTM variations.
Greff et al. (2015) performed an extensive experimental comparison called 'LSTM: A Search Space Odyssey'.
Greff et al. (2015) showed that some significantly simpler LSTM architectures with one gate fewer perform nearly as well as the vanilla LSTM.
GRU (Gated Recurrent Unit) was developed by Cho et al. (2014).
GRU implements the constant error carousel.
GRU is simpler than LSTM.
GRU merges cell state and hidden state.
GRU uses two gates: update gate and reset gate.
GRU update gate: $u_t = \sigma(W_{xu} x_t + W_{hu} h_{t-1} + b_u)$.
GRU reset gate: $r_t = \sigma(W_{xr} x_t + W_{hr} h_{t-1} + b_r)$.
GRU candidate hidden state: $h'_t = \tanh(W_{xh'} x_t + W_{hh'} (r_t \odot h_{t-1}))$.
GRU hidden state update: $h_t = (1 - u_t) \odot h'_t + u_t \odot h_{t-1}$.
GRU uses fewer weight matrices than LSTM: 6 weight matrices vs. 8 for standard LSTM or 11 for LSTM with peephole connections.
GRU uses fewer parameters than LSTM.
GRU is only slightly worse than LSTM in performance.
More GRUs can be fit under a given computational budget compared to LSTM.
Other RNN variations exist besides LSTM and GRU.
Józefowicz, Zaremba, and Sutskever (2015) performed a huge evolutionary search over RNN architectures.
Józefowicz et al. (2015) identified several interesting alternative RNN structures.

transcript.text: The main advantage of convolutional neural networks is weight reuse.
In convolutional neural networks, the same weights are applied over the entire input.
The same weights are applied across all intermediate feature tensors (outputs of intermediate layers).
Weight reuse enables parallel processing.
Weight reuse drastically reduces the number of parameters.

In classical computer vision, before neural networks, convolutions were used as handcrafted filters applied in parallel over an image for tasks such as sharpening, blurring, adding contrast, embossing, and edge detection.
Gabor filters perform directed edge detection by computing discrete derivatives (finite differences) in different directions.
One Gabor filter activates on large vertical differences between adjacent pixels.
Another Gabor filter activates on horizontal changes.
Applying max pooling as an image filter clamps to maximum brightness and produces a strange result.
Applying average pooling as an image filter appears smoother.
The purpose of average pooling is not to produce a smoother image.
In ResNet-18, the first layer’s convolutional filters can be examined.
Some first-layer filters in ResNet-18 detect diagonal or vertical lines.
Other first-layer filters in ResNet-18 identify colors or color gradients.
With an input image, one first-layer filter in ResNet-18 might fire where green appears (e.g., grass or trees).
Another first-layer filter might fire for horizontal edges.
Deeper in ResNet-18, the direct pixel-to-feature correspondence vanishes.
Deeper in ResNet-18, each feature has a receptive field.
Pinpointing the exact contributing pixels for a deep feature requires additional math.
It is possible to observe what upper-layer features in ResNet-18 respond to.
In ResNet-18, the second layer fires for high-frequency content such as stripes and edges across the image.
Deeper layers in ResNet-18 activate for more semantic, salient objects.
A deep filter in ResNet-18 might fire for eyes and ear tips.
Even deeper filters in ResNet-18 respond to entire heads.
Visualizations of deep features become increasingly blurry and less geometric.
Deep features can be mapped back to the original image to approximate their triggers.
At a deep layer in ResNet-18, one can find features strongly selective for specific classes.
Cat-selectivity in ResNet-18 means that the feature’s activation correlates strongly with the 'cat' class, as trained on ImageNet.
Inputting a half-cat, half-dog image causes the cat-selective feature to fire on the cat half.
Inputting a half-cat, half-dog image causes the dog-selective feature to fire on the dog half.
GradCAM is a more detailed interpretation method.
In a classification network, the output is a set of probabilities per class.
Running GradCAM on a specific class output reveals which pixels contributed most to that output value.
For instance, in GradCAM, the 'Egyptian cat' output responds due to certain image pixels.
GradCAM is not an attention mechanism.
GradCAM provides an explanation for the network's decision.
In the cat-dog image, the Egyptian cat output focuses on cat pixels.
In the cat-dog image, the Blenheim-Spaniel output focuses on dog pixels.
AlexNet was the most important convolutional architecture in history.
AlexNet was the first truly effective convolutional network.
AlexNet dominated the ImageNet large-scale visual recognition competition by an extraordinary margin.
In 2011/2012, competing methods in the ImageNet competition had error rates around 22–23%.
AlexNet achieved an error rate of approximately 13% in the ImageNet competition.
The following year, the entire ImageNet leaderboard switched to convolutional networks.
After AlexNet, classical computer vision was abandoned for image classification.
AlexNet’s first key technical idea is that it is split into two parallel streams.
AlexNet was the first industrial-scale instance of model parallelization.
Model parallelization is a very important concept in deep learning.
To train with multiple GPUs, there are two main approaches: data parallelization and model parallelization.
Data parallelization splits a mini-batch across GPUs.
In data parallelization, the mini-batch parts are processed in parallel on different GPUs.
In data parallelization, the results from GPUs are collected.
In data parallelization, a single update is performed based on all weight updates.
In data parallelization, the network implementation does not change.
Data parallelization increases the effective mini-batch size by spreading the batch.
Model parallelization assumes the model does not fit on one GPU.
In model parallelization, you split the model across GPUs.
AlexNet, implemented by Alex Krizhevsky in 2011 and published in 2012, used model parallelization by hand.
Implementing model parallelization by hand was a major engineering feat at the time.
Today, frameworks like PyTorch allow assigning specific weight matrices to specific GPUs.
PyTorch automatically handles communication in model parallelization.
When designing a model-parallel network, you want to minimize cross-GPU communication because it is slower than on-chip communication.
For instance, a model-parallel design might have only two points where the GPUs exchange information.
AlexNet was the breakthrough moment for convolutional networks.
After AlexNet, the field of convolutional networks exploded.
Many improvements in convolutional networks followed from relatively simple ideas.
The first improvement after AlexNet was VGG.
AlexNet used $11 \times 11$ convolutions in the first layer.
Now we rarely see $11 \times 11$ convolutions.
VGG showed that large convolutions can be represented as compositions of small ones, typically stacks of $3 \times 3$ (sometimes $5 \times 5$).
Using stacks of small convolutions instead of large ones is like a convolution inside a convolution.
Using stacks of small convolutions further reduces the number of weights.
Using stacks of small convolutions acts as additional structural regularization.
Structural regularization from small convolution stacks works because the network processes different parts of the input in the same way.
VGG's approach usually works better than using large convolutions.
The second improvement idea is Inception (GoogLeNet).
Inception is part of the broader concept of Network in Network.
In Network in Network, an image tile is processed by a small neural network consisting of a single weight matrix applied to the concatenated input.
The inception trick replaces the simple convolution in a Network-in-Network with a more complex mini-network.
The inception mini-network is still applied identically across tiles.
Inception units often feature multiple parallel processing branches.
The use of multiple parallel branches in inception units is not a coincidence.
The third and most important improvement idea is residual connections.
Residual connections give rise to ResNet.
If a layer’s output $f(x)$ saturates, its gradients vanish.
Without a skip connection, if a layer's gradients vanish, all layers below stop receiving gradients because gradients flow through derivatives that go to zero.
The residual connection adds the input to the output: $y = f(x) + x$.
When $f(x)$ stops learning, gradients still flow through the identity path.
Kaiming He introduced ResNets.
Kaiming He called ResNets the 'revolution of depth.'
With residual connections, networks with hundreds of layers could be trained.
AlexNet had 8 trainable layers.
VGG had 19 trainable layers.
GoogLeNet had 22 trainable layers.
ResNet immediately reached 150 layers.
With residual connections, you could go to 200, 500, or even 1000 layers without training issues.
The only limit to increasing depth with residual connections is diminishing returns.
Practical ResNets go to about 200 layers.
The bottleneck idea reduces weight count further, similar to VGG.
VGG replaced a large $n \times n$ convolution, which has $n^2$ weights, by a sequence of small convolutions, which have linear in $n$ weights.
Convolutions already save a huge number of weights.
We can reduce weight count even further.
The input to a standard convolutional layer is a 3D tensor.
In a standard convolutional layer, the operation is replicated over the full input.
In a standard convolutional layer, a cut-out window has depth $D$, width $W$, and height $H$.
A standard convolutional layer produces a single feature vector of size $D'$.
The weight tensor of a standard convolutional layer has dimensions $D \times W \times H \times D'$.
The convolutional layer has far fewer parameters than a fully connected layer.
The parameter count of a convolutional layer can still grow quickly.
For a convolutional layer with $D = 256$, $D' = 256$, and $W = H = 3$, the weight tensor is $256 \times 3 \times 3 \times 256$, which is about 590K parameters.
Instead of a full convolution with $D \times D' \times 9$ weights, the bottleneck idea first compresses the features with a $1 \times 1$ convolution.
After the $1 \times 1$ compression, the bottleneck idea does the spatial convolution.
After the spatial convolution, the bottleneck idea expands back with another $1 \times 1$ convolution.
In the bottleneck idea, an input of size $D \times W \times H$ is passed through a $1 \times 1$ convolution that reduces depth to $D''$, for example 32.
Then a spatial convolution of size $W \times H$ is applied.
Finally, another $1 \times 1$ convolution restores the depth to $D'$, for example 256.
The parameter count of the bottleneck block is $D \cdot D'' + D'' \cdot W \cdot H \cdot D'' + D'' \cdot D'$.
For $D=256$, $D''=32$, $W=3$, $H=3$, the parameter count is $256 \times 32 + 32 \times 32 \times 9 + 32 \times 256 = 25,600$.
The original full convolution parameter count is approximately 590,000.
The bottleneck block achieves about a 25-fold saving in parameters.
In a single-branch bottleneck, a 256-dimensional feature vector is compressed to 32 numbers.
The decompression from 32 numbers back to 256 cannot restore the lost information.
In a single branch, the bottleneck idea makes no sense.
One could simply let the previous layer produce 32 features instead and save even more weights.
The bottleneck idea alone does not work.
The bottleneck idea never appears alone in practice.
The bottleneck idea becomes useful when multiple parallel branches are used.
In the split-transform-merge approach, several copies of the bottleneck block are created.
Each parallel branch has its own independently learned weights.
The outputs of the parallel branches are concatenated.
With $D=256$ and bottleneck $D''=32$, eight parallel branches are needed to reconstruct a 256-dimensional output.
The total parameter count for eight branches is approximately 205,000.
This results in about a 3–4-fold saving compared to the original 590,000 parameters.
Geometrically, the parallel branches take multiple different projections of the same high-dimensional feature space.
Each projection captures a different aspect of the data.
The split-transform-merge network can be trained to avoid losing important information.
The split-transform-merge network can even outperform processing the entire high-dimensional object at once.
Doing many random projections of a high-dimensional object is often a good idea.
In the split-transform-merge, the projections are learned to be useful, which is even better.
The approach is called split-transform-merge.
In split-transform-merge, first the input is split, then each part is transformed, then the results are merged.
Split-transform-merge is a standard idea in convolutional architectures.
ResNeXt is an example of split-transform-merge.
ResNeXt is now outdated, about 10 years old.
In ResNeXt, 256 channels are split into 32 paths of width 4.
ResNeXt implements multiple extreme projections that work better together.
The Inception and Inception-ResNet families were a highly important line of networks.
For a long time, Inception and Inception-ResNet served as the best backbones for various computer vision tasks.
When tackling tasks like object detection or segmentation, there is rarely enough labeled data to train a network from scratch.
The standard practice is to use a backbone pretrained on ImageNet for classification.
The classification head of the pretrained backbone is cut off.
The rest of the network is used as a feature extractor.
The feature extractor may be fine-tuned slightly.
The Inception-ResNet family was one of the most influential backbones around 2016.
The main idea of Inception-ResNet was to design progressively better basic blocks.
Basic blocks are small neural networks that process the inputs.
Another important advance was replacing pooling layers with learnable reduction blocks.
Max pooling can be used to reduce spatial dimension, e.g., from 256×256 to 128×128.
It is better to let a trainable layer do more interesting work for spatial reduction.
Trainable reduction is achieved by composing layers with strided convolutions so that the output becomes smaller.
Reduction blocks sometimes contain pooling internally.
Reduction blocks follow the split-transform-merge pattern.
In reduction blocks, several parallel processing lines produce results that are merged.
Adding residual connections to Inception yields Inception-ResNet.
Inception-ResNet V2 was a very influential and widely used backbone.
There were ideas to further reduce network size and the number of layers.
Two objectives must be balanced: memory (number of weights) and latency (number of layers).
A smaller network reduces memory.
Latency depends more on the number of layers because operations within a layer are parallelized on the GPU.
The number of sequential steps matters most for latency.
The size of intermediate representations also plays a role in latency.
Latency is critical for real-time applications such as surveillance tracking.
Surveillance tracking must run at least 30–60 fps.
SqueezeNet targeted efficiency goals.
MobileNet targeted efficiency goals.
MobileNet was designed specifically to bring computer vision to mobile devices.
EfficientNet topped the architectural progress in efficient convolutional networks.
EfficientNet's design was found automatically via large-scale neural architecture search.
The neural architecture search considered how to scale a convolutional network.
The three main scaling knobs are depth (number of layers), width (number of channels), and resolution (input size).
When scaling, if depth grows exponentially with exponent α, width with β, and resolution with γ, the total number of weights scales as their product.
They ran an evolutionary search to find the optimal balance of α, β, and γ.
The resulting EfficientNet family defined the state of the art across the field.
In the plot, the x-axis is the number of parameters (fewer is better).
In the plot, the y-axis is ImageNet top-1 accuracy (higher is better).
The best networks lie in the top left corner of the plot, representing small size and high accuracy.
Large networks generally achieve higher accuracy than small networks, indicating a trade-off.
The Pareto frontier shows, for each model size, the highest accuracy achievable.
The Pareto frontier shows, for each target accuracy, the smallest model size needed.
The EfficientNet family achieved state-of-the-art performance across all sizes, effectively defining the Pareto frontier.
Since the introduction of EfficientNet, there has been no revolution in convolutional network architectures.
The research community has largely switched to using transformers.
EfficientNet remains the best underlying convolutional architecture.
EfficientNet serves as the backbone for many object detection and segmentation pipelines.
Those pipelines achieve state-of-the-art results.
Batch normalization computes the mean of a feature over spatial dimensions and mini-batch examples.
Layer normalization does not average over the mini-batch dimension.
In layer normalization, with batch size one, normalization is performed over all features of a single sample, producing one statistic per layer.
Transformers commonly use layer normalization because they are large and often trained with small mini-batches.
Layer norm provides normalization within a single training sample.
Before transformers, the two main deep learning architectures were convolutional networks and recurrent networks.
Recurrent networks are designed for sequential data.
Images are two-dimensional structures, making CNNs a natural choice.
Input data often comes as sequences.
Time series data (e.g., financial data) is a sequence.
Sound is a sequence of amplitude ticks.
In classical ML, raw amplitude sequences are too long to process directly.
Sound is often preprocessed by cutting into 20-30 ms packets and extracting features, resulting in a sequence of feature vectors.
Text is a sequence of tokens with a one-dimensional structure.
Sequence-to-single output tasks, like text classification, take a sequence (e.g., news article) and output one label (e.g., topic).
Sequence generation tasks take a non-sequential input (like an image) and produce an output sequence (like a caption).
Sequence-to-sequence problems have both input and output as sequences, e.g., machine translation.
Sequence labeling produces an output sequence aligned with the input, such as part-of-speech tagging.
Subtitle generation from video is a sequence labeling task where each frame gets corresponding text.
Object tracking is a sequence labeling task where segmentation is applied per frame to track an object.
CNNs are not inherently well-suited for sequences.
Convolutional approaches to NLP were competitive with recurrent approaches before transformers became dominant.
CNNs lack the ability to recall information from long past in a sequence, which is necessary for understanding full sentences.
Understanding a paragraph requires remembering earlier context.
In RNNs, each input $x_t$ is processed by a small neural network called a recurrent unit.
The recurrent unit takes a new input $x$ and a hidden state $h$ as inputs.
The unit updates the hidden state to capture the sequence up to the current input, assuming the previous hidden state captured earlier context.
The recurrent unit is defined as a function $f(x, h)$ that outputs an updated hidden state $h'$ and optionally an output.
The hidden state is a vector that accumulates relevant information about the sequence.
The hidden state is initialized as $h_0$, then updated to $h_1, h_2,$ etc.
In classical RNNs, the hidden state update is $h' = g(Ax + Bh)$, with weight matrices $A$ and $B$ and activation $g$ (e.g., tanh, ELU).
RNNs date back to the late 1980s.
Initially, RNNs could not be trained properly due to insufficient compute.
A unidirectional RNN processes the sequence from left to right.
For whole-sequence classification, using the final hidden state of a unidirectional RNN may be sufficient.
For sequence labeling like part-of-speech tagging, a unidirectional RNN only sees preceding context, which is limiting.
Bidirectional RNNs consist of two separate RNNs: one processing left-to-right, the other right-to-left.
The two hidden states from bidirectional RNNs are merged to predict $y_t$, incorporating both past and future context.
Bidirectional RNNs should be used unless the task prohibits it.
Language modeling requires a unidirectional model because it predicts the next word from left context only.
Real-time object tracking may require a unidirectional network due to limited future visibility.
In sequence-to-sequence tasks, bidirectional RNNs are standard because the full input can be read before output.
In RNN training for sequence classification, the loss is computed from the final output prediction compared to the true label.
In an RNN, the weights (e.g., matrix $W$) are shared across all time steps.
Separate weight matrices per time step would make training infeasible.
Weight sharing enables processing sequences of arbitrary length.
The gradient w.r.t. a weight $w$ is the sum of its influence over all time steps: $\frac{\partial L}{\partial w_t} + \frac{\partial L}{\partial w_{t-1}} + \dots + \frac{\partial L}{\partial w_1}$.
The weight is reused at each time step in the computational graph, not separate weights.
Weight sharing, as in CNNs, allows sparse activations to build meaningful gradients.
In a simplified linear recurrence without activations or inputs, the hidden state evolves as $H_T = W^T H_0$.
The spectral radius $\rho$ of $W$ controls the scaling: $\|H_t\| \approx \rho^t \|H_0\|$.
If $\rho > 1$, activations explode exponentially, causing numerical overflow.
In the backward pass, multiplication by $W^\top$ similarly leads to sensitivity to $\rho$.
Exploding gradients occur when $\rho > 1$; vanishing gradients occur when $\rho < 1$.
Vanishing gradients cause loss of long-term memory because early inputs' influence decays exponentially.
Exploding gradients cause training failure; vanishing gradients degrade performance but are not catastrophic.
Exploding gradients can be fixed by gradient clipping.
If the gradient norm exceeds a threshold, scale it down to the threshold.
Clipping is applied repeatedly during training.
Gradient clipping is the only solution needed for exploding gradients.
Pascanu published a paper in 2013 studying RNN behavior.
The Pascanu paper provides insights into activation and weight dynamics during RNN training, not new architectures.
In the loss landscape, exploding gradients correspond to a region with a steep cliff where gradients become huge.
Without clipping, large gradients cause divergence.
With clipping, the updates stay in a normal regime and proceed in roughly the right direction.
Gradient clipping is a theoretically and practically sound method that preserves the descent direction.

summary.text: Weight reuse is the defining advantage of convolutional neural networks (CNNs).
In CNNs, the same filters are applied across the entire input and over all intermediate feature tensors.
Weight reuse dramatically reduces the number of parameters.
Weight reuse enables massive parallelism.
Before deep learning, convolutions were used as handcrafted filters in classical computer vision.
In classical computer vision, small matrices were slid over an image to perform operations such as sharpening, blurring, embossing, or edge detection.
Gabor filters compute discrete directional derivatives.
One Gabor filter fires on large vertical differences between adjacent pixels.
Another Gabor filter fires on horizontal changes.
Applying max pooling as an image filter would clamp to maximum brightness, producing unnatural results.
Average pooling appears smoother but is not meant to be a pixel-level transformation.
In ResNet-18, the first layer's convolutional filters can be inspected.
Some first-layer filters in ResNet-18 detect diagonal or vertical lines.
Some first-layer filters in ResNet-18 respond to colors or colour gradients.
In ResNet-18, when an input image is passed through, one filter might fire where green appears.
In ResNet-18, another filter might fire for horizontal edges.
Deeper in the network, direct pixel-to-feature correspondence disappears.
Each unit in a CNN has a receptive field.
Tracing exactly which pixels contribute to a unit's activation requires additional mathematics.
One can observe what upper-layer features respond to.
In ResNet-18, the second layer activates on high-frequency content (stripes, edges) across the whole image.
Deeper layers in ResNet-18 respond to more semantic structures: a filter might detect eyes and ear tips.
Even deeper filters in ResNet-18 fire on entire heads.
Visualizations of deeper features become progressively blurrier and less geometric.
The features can be mapped back to the original image to approximate what triggers them.
At a late layer, features can be strongly class-selective.
A cat-selective feature correlates strongly with the "cat" class on ImageNet.
If a composite image half-cat, half-dog is presented, the cat-selective feature fires on the cat half and a dog-selective feature fires on the dog half.
This demonstrates genuine selectivity.
GradCAM is a more detailed explanation method.
Given a classification network, running GradCAM on a specific class output reveals which pixels contributed most to that output value.
For example, the "Egyptian cat" logit in a network responds because of certain image regions, while the "Blenheim Spaniel" logit focuses on other regions.
GradCAM is not an attention mechanism.
GradCAM provides a post-hoc explanation of the network's decision.
AlexNet (Krizhevsky, Sutskever, Hinton, 2012) was the architecture that kick-started modern deep learning for computer vision.
AlexNet dominated the ImageNet Large-Scale Visual Recognition Competition by an extraordinary margin.
In the ImageNet Large-Scale Visual Recognition Competition, competing methods had error rates around 22–23%.
AlexNet achieved an error rate of approximately 13% in that competition.
The following year, the entire leaderboard of the competition switched to convolutional networks.
Classical computer vision was abandoned for image classification.
Model parallelism was used for the first time at an industrial scale in AlexNet.
In AlexNet, the network was split into two parallel streams, each running on a separate GPU.
Data parallelism splits a mini-batch across GPUs, processes them in parallel, and then aggregates the gradients for a single update.
In data parallelism, the network implementation does not change.
Model parallelism is necessary when the model does not fit on a single GPU.
AlexNet was hand-engineered by Alex Krizhevsky to explicitly assign layers to different GPUs while minimising cross-GPU communication.
Cross-GPU communication is slower than on-chip communication.
In modern frameworks such as PyTorch, specific weight matrices can be assigned to specific GPUs and communication is handled automatically.
VGG (Oxford Visual Geometry Group) represents large convolutions as compositions of smaller ones, typically stacks of $3 \times 3$ convolutions.
Using a stack of $3 \times 3$ filters reduces the number of weights compared to one large filter.
Using a stack of $3 \times 3$ filters makes the network deeper.
Using a stack of $3 \times 3$ filters acts as additional structural regularisation because the network processes different parts of the input in the same way.
VGG was used in the ILSVRC-2014 competition.
NVIDIA later optimised GPUs especially for $3 \times 3$ convolutions.
The idea of treating a large convolution as a "convolution inside a convolution" proved very effective.
The Inception architecture and its realisation in GoogLeNet employ the "network in network" concept to reduce the number of weights even further.
Instead of using a single linear convolution over a tile, Inception units implement a more complex mini-network that is still applied identically across all spatial positions.
Another idea in Inception is to insert additional classifiers (and corresponding auxiliary loss terms) at intermediate layers of the network.
Inception units frequently feature multiple parallel processing branches.
In Inception v2 (Szegedy et al., 2015), $n \times n$ convolutions are replaced by $n \times 1$ followed by $1 \times n$ convolutions.
In Inception v2, filter banks become wider rather than deeper.
The same paper that introduced Inception v2 also introduced Inception v3.
Inception v3 adds RMSProp optimisation.
Inception v3 adds factorised $7 \times 7$ convolutions.
Inception v3 adds batch normalisation in the auxiliary classifiers.
Inception v3 adds label smoothing.
A regular classifier trains the softmax with a hard target $q(k) = [k = y]$ (a one-hot vector).
The hard target encourages the logits to grow without bound, leading to overconfident predictions and overfitting.
Label smoothing replaces the hard target with a soft target: $q'(k) = (1 - \epsilon)[k = y] + \epsilon u(k)$.
In the soft target, $u(k)$ is a prior distribution, often the uniform distribution $u(k) = \frac{1}{K}$.
Label smoothing prevents the network from becoming too certain and improves generalisation.
Residual learning addresses the vanishing gradient problem by training differences rather than the full mapping.
A residual unit computes $y^{(k)} = F(x^{(k)}) + x^{(k)}$.
In the residual unit, $x^{(k)}$ is the input to layer $k$.
In the residual unit, $F$ is the function learned by the layer.
In the residual unit, $y^{(k)}$ becomes $x^{(k+1)}$.
The gradient can flow directly through the identity path in a residual unit: $\frac{\partial y^{(k)}}{\partial x^{(k)}} = 1 + \frac{\partial F(x^{(k)})}{\partial x^{(k)}}$.
Because of the identity path, gradients do not vanish when $F$ saturates.
When a layer's output $F(x)$ saturates and its derivatives approach zero, without a skip connection all layers below would stop receiving gradients.
The identity shortcut in residual units guarantees a path for gradient flow, enabling extremely deep networks.
Kaiming He introduced ResNets.
Kaiming He called the introduction of ResNets the "revolution of depth".
AlexNet had 8 trainable layers.
VGG had 19 trainable layers.
GoogLeNet had 22 trainable layers.
ResNet immediately scaled to 150 layers.
After ResNet, networks of 200, 500, or even 1000 layers became trainable.
Practical ResNets typically go up to about 200 layers.
Highway networks (Schmidhuber) are a related approach to residual learning.
In highway networks, the output is a gated combination: $y^{(k)} = C(x^{(k)}) x^{(k)} + T(x^{(k)}) F(x^{(k)})$.
In highway networks, $C$ is a carry gate and $T$ is a transform gate.
In highway networks, usually $C = 1 - T$.
In practice, residual connections work best when they are as "straight" as possible.
Beyond the weight reduction achieved by VGG-style small filters, an even more aggressive parameter saving is possible via bottleneck layers.
A standard convolutional layer operates on a cut-out window of depth $D$, width $W$, height $H$, producing an output of depth $D'$.
The weight tensor size of a standard convolutional layer is $D \times W \times H \times D'$.
With small filters ($W = H = 3$) and moderate depths ($D = D' = 256$), a standard convolutional layer has approximately $256 \times 3 \times 3 \times 256 \approx 590\text{k}$ parameters.
A bottleneck layer first compresses the input channel depth with a $1 \times 1$ convolution to a much smaller dimension $D''$.
Then the bottleneck applies the spatial convolution.
Finally the bottleneck expands back to $D'$ with another $1 \times 1$ convolution.

If $D=256$, $D''=32$, $D'=256$, the parameter count of a bottleneck becomes $D \cdot D'' + D'' \cdot W \cdot H \cdot D'' + D'' \cdot D' = 256 \cdot 32 + 32 \cdot 32 \cdot 9 + 32 \cdot 256 \approx 25.6\text{k}$.
This parameter count is a 25-fold reduction compared to the full convolution without bottleneck.
Compressing a 256-dimensional feature vector down to 32 numbers and then decompressing back to 256 cannot restore lost information.
A single bottleneck branch would be senseless because one could simply let the previous layer produce 32 features instead and save even more weights.
The bottleneck idea becomes powerful when multiple parallel branches are used.

By creating several copies of the bottleneck block, each with its own independently learned weights, and concatenating their outputs, the network learns multiple low-dimensional projections of the same high-dimensional space.
The multiple low-dimensional projections learned by the parallel bottleneck branches capture different aspects of the data.

With $D=256$, $D''=32$, and 8 branches, the total parameter cost of the multiple bottlenecks is about $8 \times 25.6\text{k} \approx 205\text{k}$, compared to the original $590\text{k}$ – a 3–4 fold saving.
Geometrically, taking many learned random projections of a high-dimensional object is often beneficial.
In the bottleneck approach, the projections are trained to be useful.
The approach of using multiple parallel bottleneck branches is called split-transform-merge: split the input, transform each part, then merge the results.
Split-transform-merge is a standard pattern in convolutional architectures.
ResNeXt (Xie et al., 2016) replaces ResNet units with split-transform-merge units reminiscent of Inception.
In ResNeXt, the input channels are divided into groups, and every group receives its own convolutions.
This grouping is akin to group convolutions, already used in AlexNet for parallelisation.
Group convolutions in ResNeXt yield a kind of specialisation in the resulting feature maps.
Another paper (Szegedy et al., 2016) introduced Inception v4 and Inception-ResNet.
The Inception family long served as excellent backbones for many computer vision tasks.

When labelled data is scarce, the standard practice is to take a model pretrained on ImageNet for classification, cut off its classification head, and use the rest as a feature extractor, possibly with light fine-tuning.
Inception v4 standardises everything and simplifies the units.
In Inception v4, a "stem" module is defined first, followed by three basic blocks (A, B, C) and special reduction blocks to reduce spatial dimensions.

In Inception v4, instead of a fixed pooling operation, the reduction blocks are learnable compositions of layers with strided convolutions, often containing pooling internally and following the split-transform-merge pattern.
Inception-ResNet adds residual connections to Inception blocks.
In Inception-ResNet, there is no pooling, but reduction blocks are still employed, making the architecture even simpler.
Inception-ResNet v2 is a refined version that performs extremely well in practice.
Inception-ResNet v2 was one of the most widely used backbones around 2016.
When deploying networks, two resources must be balanced: memory (number of weights) and latency (number of sequential layers).
GPU parallelism means that the number of layers often dictates latency more than the raw parameter count.
Intermediate representation sizes also matter for deployment.
Real-time applications, such as surveillance tracking, require at least 30-60 frames per second.
The need for real-time performance drives the development of extremely efficient architectures.
SqueezeNet (Iandola et al., 2017) aims to drastically reduce the number of parameters.
SqueezeNet replaces $3 \times 3$ filters with $1 \times 1$ filters.
SqueezeNet reduces the number of input channels for the remaining $3 \times 3$ convolutions.
SqueezeNet delays downsampling as late as possible to keep activation maps large.
The core building block of SqueezeNet is the fire module.
The fire module is composed of a squeeze layer (only $1 \times 1$ convolutions) followed by an expand layer (a mix of $1 \times 1$ and $3 \times 3$ convolutions).
SqueezeNet yields about 50× fewer parameters than AlexNet, at the cost of some accuracy.
MobileNet (Howard et al., 2017) designs networks specifically for mobile devices.
MobileNet uses depthwise separable convolutions.
A depthwise separable convolution decomposes a standard convolution into a depthwise convolution (one filter per input channel) followed by a $1 \times 1$ convolution.
The depthwise separable structure is more complex but has far fewer weights than a standard convolution.
The overall MobileNet architecture is not very deep.
MobileNet saves many parameters with a small drop in quality.
EfficientNet (Tan, Le, 2019) applies neural architecture search to find state-of-the-art networks.
The key insight of EfficientNet is compound scaling.
Simultaneously scaling network depth, width, and input resolution yields better performance than scaling a single dimension.
The neural architecture search in EfficientNet considers exponential scaling with exponents $\alpha$ (depth), $\beta$ (width) and $\gamma$ (resolution).
In EfficientNet, the total number of weights scales as the product of the scaling exponents $\alpha$, $\beta$, and $\gamma$.
The efficiency landscape is often displayed on a plot with number of parameters on the x‑axis (fewer is better) and ImageNet top‑1 accuracy on the y‑axis (higher is better).
The Pareto frontier connects the best possible network for every size, and for every target quality the smallest possible network.
The EfficientNet family succeeded in defining this frontier.
EfficientNet remains the best underlying convolutional backbone.
EfficientNet is widely used in object detection and segmentation pipelines.
As weights of a layer change during training, the distribution of its outputs shifts.
The next layer must then continually re‑adapt.
Neurons that have reached saturation slow down retraining.
Internal covariate shift seriously impedes deep network training.

A layer that adds a bias $b$ to its input $u$, producing $x = u + b$, if normalised by subtracting the mean, $\hat{x} = x - \mathbb{E}[x]$, and then updating $b := b + \Delta b$, the normalised output does not change: $u + b + \Delta b - \mathbb{E}[u + b + \Delta b] = u + b - \mathbb{E}[u + b]$.
The biases grow without bound while the normalised output remains unchanged.
Training fails in this scenario.
Normalisation as a layer $\hat{x} = \text{Norm}(x, X)$ requires the entire dataset $X$ to compute gradients $\frac{\partial \text{Norm}}{\partial x}$ and $\frac{\partial \text{Norm}}{\partial X}$.
Normalisation as a layer requires computing the full covariance matrix $\text{Cov}[x] = \mathbb{E}_{x \in X}[xx^\top] - \mathbb{E}[x]\mathbb{E}[x]^\top$.
Computing the full covariance matrix is computationally prohibitive.
Batch normalisation normalises each feature component separately over the current mini‑batch.
For a component $x_k$, $\hat{x}_k = \frac{x_k - \mathbb{E}[x_k]}{\sqrt{\text{Var}[x_k]}}$.
The statistics $\mathbb{E}[x_k]$ and $\text{Var}[x_k]$ are computed on the current mini‑batch.
Normalising forces the activations into the linear regime of nonlinearities (e.g., the sigmoid).
Forcing activations into the linear regime can destroy the network’s capacity.
To remedy the destruction of capacity, learnable shift and scale parameters are introduced.
The learnable shift and scale parameters are: $y_k = \gamma_k \hat{x}_k + \beta_k = \gamma_k \frac{x_k - \mathbb{E}[x_k]}{\sqrt{\text{Var}[x_k]}} + \beta_k$.
$\gamma_k$ and $\beta_k$ are trained jointly with all other network weights.
Although originally motivated by reducing internal covariate shift, subsequent research showed that BN’s effectiveness does not really depend on this.
BN provides regularisation.
BN makes dropout often unnecessary.
BN significantly improves training.
One possible explanation for BN's effectiveness is that BN smooths the gradients, reducing the Lipschitz constant (Santurkar et al., 2019).
Another possible explanation is that BN decouples the learning of the direction and length of weight vectors, which improves training dynamics.
Yet another possible explanation is that BN helps achieve linear convergence in ordinary gradient descent.
Many normalisation methods share the same general operations: compute statistics over some set, normalise, then apply a learned scale and shift.
Normalisation methods differ in which dimensions the statistics are computed over.
The general form is: compute mean and variance over a specified set of axes, normalise, then transform with $\gamma$ and $\beta$.
Batch Normalization computes statistics over the mini‑batch dimension ($N$).
Batch Normalization is commonly used for images.
Batch Normalization averages the same feature over spatial dimensions and across the mini‑batch.
Layer Normalization computes statistics over all channels and spatial dimensions of a layer (all features of a single sample).
Layer Normalization does not average over the mini‑batch.
Layer Normalization is used mostly for vectors, in particular in transformers.
When using layer norm, the mini‑batch size is often one, so no mini‑batch statistics are available.
Layer norm normalises over the whole tensor of features for one sample.
Layer norm is essential for transformers, where large models rarely allow large mini‑batches.
Instance Normalization computes statistics over the spatial dimensions ($H$, $W$) only, separately per sample and per channel.
Instance Normalization is used, e.g., in AdaIN for style transfer.
Group Normalization splits channels into groups and normalises over each group together with the spatial dimensions.
Weight Standardization standardises the weights (per output channel) instead of normalising activations.
Weight Standardization effectively normalises the gradients during backpropagation.
Group norm combined with weight standardisation was used in BiT (Big Transfer).
Batch normalisation is not effective for recurrent networks (Laurent et al., 2016).
Recurrent batch normalisation was proposed (Cooijmans et al., 2016).
Weight normalisation (Salimans and Kingma, 2016) re‑parameterises the weight vector as $h_i = f\!\left(\frac{\gamma}{\|w_i\|} w_i^\top x + b_i\right)$.
Weight normalisation rescales the gradient, stabilises its norm, and brings the covariance matrix closer to the identity.
The landscape of normalisation methods remains an active research area (Huang et al., 2020).
Many problems involve sequential data: financial time series, sound, or text.
Unlike images, which are two‑dimensional structures naturally suited to CNNs, sequences are inherently one‑dimensional.
Sequence → single output: e.g., text classification – an entire news article is mapped to one category (sports, politics, science).
Single input → sequence: e.g., image captioning – a still image is converted into a variable‑length text description.
Sequence → sequence: e.g., machine translation – both input and output are sequences of variable length.
Sequence labelling: the output is a label for each input element, aligned with the input.

Examples of sequence labelling include part‑of‑speech tagging (a label for every word), video subtitle addition (each frame gets a text), and object tracking (segmenting an object consistently across video frames).
Applying a sliding window over the sequence cannot capture long‑range dependencies.
When reading a paragraph, one needs to remember what occurred many words earlier for the ending to make sense.
The crucial missing capability is the ability to retain information across arbitrary time spans.
Recurrent neural networks (RNNs) maintain a hidden state updated as each element is processed.
The computational graph appears to contain cycles ($s_i = h(x_i, x_{i+1}, \dots, s_{i-1})$).
Backpropagation is performed by unrolling the recurrence in time: $y_6 = f(x_3, x_4, x_5, h(x_2, x_3, x_4, h(x_1, x_2, x_3, s_0)))$.
Practically, an RNN is a very deep network with many shared weights, causing notorious training difficulties.
A recurrent unit takes an input $x_t$ and the previous hidden state $h_{t-1}$ and outputs an updated hidden state $h_t$.
The same function with the exact same weights is applied at every time step.
Weight sharing enables the network to process sequences of arbitrary length.
A classical simple RNN cell is given by $h_t = g(A x_t + B h_{t-1})$.
In the formula, $A$ and $B$ are weight matrices and $g$ is a nonlinear activation such as $\tanh$ or ELU.
In slide notation, the RNN is written as $a_t = b + W s_{t-1} + U x_t$, $s_t = f(a_t)$, $o_t = c + V s_t$, $y_t = h(o_t)$.
In the slide notation, $f$ is the recurrent nonlinearity and $h$ the output function.
Weight sharing across time allows the same weights to handle variable‑length inputs.
Weight sharing is also a source of difficulty: the gradient of the loss with respect to a weight $w$ is a large sum because $w$ participates at every time step.
The influence of $w$ passes through repeated multiplication by the same weight matrix.
Because the state is repeatedly multiplied by $W$, the dynamics are governed by the spectral radius $\rho$ of $W$.
The spectral radius $\rho$ is roughly the factor by which multiplication scales vector length.
In the simplified case $h_t \approx W^t h_0$, we have $\|h_t\| \approx \rho^t \|h_0\|$.
If $\rho > 1$, activations and gradients explode exponentially with sequence length.
If $\rho > 1$, the explosion causes numerical overflow.
If $\rho < 1$, gradients vanish as they travel backwards.
Vanishing gradients destroy the influence of early sequence elements and prevent learning of long‑term dependencies.
Exploding gradients are handled by gradient clipping.
In gradient clipping, if the gradient norm exceeds a threshold, the gradient vector is rescaled so that its norm equals the threshold.
Gradient clipping can be thought of as keeping the update from flying off a steep “wall” in the loss landscape and gently redirecting it back to the normal regime.
Pascanu et al. (2013) studied this behaviour and showed that RNNs have bifurcation points where such instabilities originate.
Clipping is theoretically and practically sound: it does not distort the direction of the gradient catastrophically.
The vanishing gradient problem is far more challenging.
The vanishing gradient problem is addressed by architectures such as LSTM and GRU.
For sequence labelling tasks, it is unnatural to look only at past context.
A bidirectional RNN runs two separate recurrent networks: one left‑to‑right, one right‑to‑left.
At position $t$, the left‑to‑right hidden state captures left context and the right‑to‑left hidden state captures right context.
The outputs of the two hidden states are merged via a classification head.
For the left-to-right RNN: $s_t = \sigma(b + W s_{t-1} + U x_t)$.
For the right-to-left RNN: $s'_t = \sigma(b' + W' s'_{t+1} + U' x_t)$.
The output is given by $o_t = c + V s_t + V' s'_t$, $y_t = h(o_t)$.
Bidirectional RNNs are standard unless the problem prohibits using future context.
Examples of problems prohibiting future context: language modelling requires predicting the next word using only left context; real‑time tracking can look only a few frames ahead.
The principle of bidirectional processing generalises to any recurrent architecture.
Vanishing gradients occur because the gradient must repeatedly pass through multiplication by $W$.
To preserve long‑term memory, a shortcut for gradients is needed, analogous to skip connections in ResNet.
The shortcut for gradients is called the constant error carousel.
LSTM (Hochreiter & Schmidhuber, 1995/1997; modern form by Gers & Schmidhuber, 2000) constructs a complex unit that explicitly controls memory.
The LSTM cell maintains a cell state $c_t$ and a hidden state $h_t$.
Gates control information flow in the LSTM cell.
Candidate cell state: $c'_t = \tanh(W_{xc} x_t + W_{hc} h_{t-1} + b_{c'})$.
Input gate: $i_t = \sigma(W_{xi} x_t + W_{hi} h_{t-1} + b_i)$.
Forget gate: $f_t = \sigma(W_{xf} x_t + W_{hf} h_{t-1} + b_f)$.
Output gate: $o_t = \sigma(W_{xo} x_t + W_{ho} h_{t-1} + b_o)$.
Cell state update: $c_t = f_t \odot c_{t-1} + i_t \odot c'_t$.
Hidden state: $h_t = o_t \odot \tanh(c_t)$.
If $f_t = 1$, then $c_t = c_{t-1} + i_t \odot c'_t$.
When $f_t = 1$, $\frac{\partial c_t}{\partial c_{t-1}} = 1$, creating the constant error carousel.
Peephole connections address the case where the output gate closes and LSTM behaviour becomes independent of the cell state.
Peephole connections add the cell state directly to the gate computations.
$i_t = \sigma(W_{xi} x_t + W_{hi} h_{t-1} + W_{pi} c_{t-1} + b_i)$.
$f_t = \sigma(W_{xf} x_t + W_{hf} h_{t-1} + W_{pf} c_{t-1} + b_f)$.
$o_t = \sigma(W_{xo} x_t + W_{ho} h_{t-1} + W_{po} c_{t-1} + b_o)$.
Numerous LSTM variations exist.
“LSTM: A Search Space Odyssey” (Greff et al., 2015) showed that some significantly simpler architectures (with one gate fewer) perform nearly as well.
GRU (Cho et al., 2014) also implements the constant error carousel but with a simpler design.
GRU merges the cell state and hidden state into a single state $h_t$.
GRU uses only two gates.
Update gate: $u_t = \sigma(W_{xu} x_t + W_{hu} h_{t-1} + b_u)$.
Reset gate: $r_t = \sigma(W_{xr} x_t + W_{hr} h_{t-1} + b_r)$.
Candidate hidden state: $h'_t = \tanh(W_{xh'} x_t + W_{hh'} (r_t \odot h_{t-1}))$.
Hidden state update: $h_t = (1 - u_t) \odot h'_t + u_t \odot h_{t-1}$.
GRU uses 6 weight matrices (vs. 8 or 11 with peepholes in LSTM).
GRU has fewer parameters than LSTM.
GRU is only slightly worse than LSTM.
Under a fixed computational budget, one can fit more GRU units, making it competitive or even preferable.
Other variations of RNN architectures exist.
Józefowicz, Zaremba, and Sutskever (2015) performed a large evolutionary search over RNN architectures.
Józefowicz, Zaremba, and Sutskever (2015) identified several interesting alternative structures.
